scenario: WIBTA for lying to my brother for the rest of our lives about having a disorder? | My brother who is 2 years younger than me has Aspberger's. We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

Asperger's is a form of autism, characterized by difficulties in social interaction and communication, and often accompanied by repetitive behaviors or intense interests. It's a spectrum disorder, meaning it affects people in different ways and to varying degrees. The brother in question is extremely intelligent, excelling in math and physics, which are areas where some people with Asperger's may have particular strengths. The brother is going through a tough time emotionally, dealing with depression and even attempting suicide. He's in outpatient treatment after being discharged from inpatient care. The person is considering lying about having Asperger's themselves to make their brother feel less alone. They believe that if they also have the disorder, it might help their brother accept his condition and not feel ashamed of it. They mention that their brother is somewhat denying his autism and that they've tried to talk to him about it without much success. They also note that their brother loves how they're becoming more alike as they get older, which might make the lie more convincing. Now, I need to evaluate whether this lie is right or wrong. To do that, I should consider the potential consequences, both positive and negative, of such a decision. On the positive side, the lie might help the brother feel supported and less isolated, which could be beneficial for his mental health. It might encourage him to accept his condition and seek help without feeling ashamed. On the negative side, lying can erode trust in a relationship. If the brother finds out that the person lied to him, it could damage their relationship severely. Trust is a fundamental component of any relationship, especially between siblings. Additionally, lying about having a disorder could trivialize the brother's experience. It might send the message that having Asperger's isn't something to be taken seriously, which could undermine the brother's efforts to understand and manage his condition. Another consideration is the potential impact on the person doing the lying. If they're not actually diagnosed with Asperger's, they might feel guilty or anxious about maintaining the lie. They could also face confusion or questions from others if the lie is discovered, which could complicate their own life and relationships. It's also important to think about alternative approaches. The brother might develop an inaccurate understanding of his own condition, or the person lying might face personal consequences that affect their own well-being. In terms of ethical considerations, honesty is generally valued in relationships because it fosters trust and mutual respect. In this case, the intention is to support the brother, but the means of achieving that support involves deception. I also need to think about the potential for the lie to backfire. If the brother ever discovers the lie, it could lead to feelings of betrayal and mistrust. Additionally, there's the question of whether the lie would actually achieve the intended effect. The brother might not necessarily accept his condition just because someone else claims to have it. In summary, while the intention behind the lie is to support and help the brother, the potential negative consequences, such as damaged trust and long-term complications, make it a risky and potentially harmful approach. There are alternative ways to provide support without resorting to deception, which might be more effective and healthier for both parties involved.
